title: Minimum Operations to Finish Jobs
statement:
There are `n` jobs that can be executed in parallel on a processor. The execution time of job `i` is `executionTime[i]`. To speed things up, the processor uses the following strategy.

In one **operation**, one job still in the pool is chosen as the **major job** and is executed for `x` seconds. Every **other** job in the pool is executed for `y` seconds, where `y < x`.

A job is complete once it has been executed for **at least** `executionTime[i]` seconds in total; it then exits the pool and takes no further part in later operations.

Find the minimum number of operations in which the processor can completely execute all the jobs if it chooses the major job optimally each time.
input_format:
The first line contains three integers `n`, `x` and `y`.
The second line contains `n` integers `executionTime[0..n-1]`.
output_format: Print a single integer: the minimum number of operations.

examples.explanation: Choose the job with time 7: the times become [1, 2, -1, 3, 4], so the job with time 1 is finished. Choose the job that now has 3 left: the remaining times drop to [-1, 0, -1, 2], so the jobs with times 4 and 3 are finished. Finally choose the last job (2 left). That is three operations. Two are not enough: after two operations every job has received at least 4 seconds, so the jobs with times 7 and 6 still need 3 and 2 more seconds. A major turn adds only `x - y = 2` extra seconds, so they need 2 + 1 = 3 major turns, more than the 2 operations available.
One operation gives the single job only 4 seconds. A second operation finishes it.

Each operation finishes at most one job outright (as the major job), while the others gain just 1 second. With 2 operations, the third job would still have 8 seconds left; with 3 operations everyone finishes.

hints: If you know the number of operations `k` in advance, you can decide whether `k` is enough. The answer is then the smallest feasible `k`, and feasibility is monotone in `k`.
With `k` operations every job gets at least `k·y` seconds for free. A job with `executionTime[i] > k·y` must be the major job `m` times, where each major turn adds only `x - y` extra seconds.

Compute `m_i = ceil((executionTime[i] - k·y) / (x - y))` for those jobs. The value `k` is feasible exactly when the sum of all `m_i` is at most `k`. Binary search `k` between 0 and `ceil(max(executionTime) / y)`.

import sys
from collections import deque

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, x, y = int(data[0]), int(data[1]), int(data[2])
t = tuple(sorted(map(int, data[3:3 + n])))
seen = {t: 0}
q = deque([t])
while q:
    s = q.popleft()
    if not s:
        print(seen[s])
        break
    for i in range(len(s)):
        nxt = tuple(sorted(r - (x if j == i else y) for j, r in enumerate(s) if r - (x if j == i else y) > 0))
        if nxt not in seen:
            seen[nxt] = seen[s] + 1
            q.append(nxt)
